recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve (2x² + 1)/(x³ − 1) into partial fractions — name each move in order.
insider_note: x³ − 1 factorises as (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) with the middle sign plus, and that quadratic must carry the numerator Bx + C; finding C = 0 at the end is correct, not a slip.

steps.label: Set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) by a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²). The quadratic x² + x + 1 has no real factors, so it gets a LINEAR numerator Bx + C.

recall.must_convey: That x³ − 1 factorises as (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) and the irreducible quadratic gets the numerator Bx + C: A/(x − 1) + (Bx + C)/(x² + x + 1).
accept: factorise x cubed minus one as x minus one into x squared plus x plus one and write A over x minus one plus Bx plus C over x squared plus x plus one
the quadratic factor cannot be split so its numerator is Bx plus C not a constant
A by x minus 1 plus Bx plus C by x square plus x plus 1

steps.why: A quadratic that cannot be factorised over the reals needs a numerator one degree lower than itself, so Bx + C. A constant alone would not give enough unknowns to match every power of x in the identity.
common_mistakes: Writing only B/(x² + x + 1) with a constant numerator over the quadratic.
Factorising x³ − 1 as (x − 1)(x² − x + 1); the middle sign is plus.
Trying to factorise x² + x + 1 further; its discriminant 1 − 4 is negative.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply by (x − 1)(x² + x + 1). A keeps the quadratic, (Bx + C) keeps (x − 1). Keep Bx + C in a bracket; it is one numerator.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying through gives 2x² + 1 = A(x² + x + 1) + (Bx + C)(x − 1).
accept: multiply both sides by x minus one into x squared plus x plus one to get two x squared plus one equals A into x squared plus x plus one plus Bx plus C into x minus one
clear the denominators so A keeps the quadratic and Bx plus C keeps x minus one
multiply through by the whole denominator to get an identity in x

Bx plus C into x minus one

steps.why: The identity is a quadratic on both sides, so it carries three pieces of information: the x² coefficient, the x coefficient and the constant. That is exactly enough for the three unknowns A, B, C.
common_mistakes: Writing Bx + C(x − 1) without the bracket, so only C is multiplied by (x − 1).
Giving A the factor (x − 1) instead of the quadratic.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Only one real root, x = 1, which gives A. B and C come from comparing coefficients: x² gives A + B, the constant term gives A − C.

recall.must_convey: That x = 1 gives A = 1, comparing x² gives A + B = 2 so B = 1, and comparing constants gives A − C = 1 so C = 0.
accept: put x equals one to get A equals one, compare x squared to get A plus B equals two so B is one, compare constants to get A minus C equals one so C is zero

steps.why: The quadratic factor has no real root to substitute, so B and C must come from coefficients. Expanding (Bx + C)(x − 1) gives Bx² + (C − B)x − C; the x² coefficient A + B and the constant A − C are the two easiest to read.
common_mistakes: Reading the constant term on the right as A + C instead of A − C; (Bx + C)(x − 1) ends in −C.
Writing B = 2 by forgetting that A also contributes to the x² coefficient.
Finding C = 0 and thinking a mistake was made; C = 0 is a correct value.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. With B = 1 and C = 0 the second numerator is just x. Write the original fraction on the left.

recall.must_convey: That the fraction equals 1/(x − 1) + x/(x² + x + 1).
accept: the answer is one over x minus one plus x over x squared plus x plus one

steps.why: The resolved form is the answer. The numerator over the quadratic is Bx + C = 1·x + 0 = x, and writing it as x rather than 1x + 0 is the expected presentation.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/(x² + x + 1) and losing the x from the numerator.
Not checking: put x = 2 in the identity, 9 = 7 + 2. If the two sides differ, a constant is wrong.
